When we write
¡ Y = Model (X), what actually happens?
¡ Step 1: Design an algorithm Model to solve a problem, with input data X.
¡ Step 2: A program expresses the algorithm. 
¡ Step 3: System software turns the program into an executable, parallel, and robust task.
¡ Step 4: Operating system schedules computing tasks and deploys them onto hardware for 
executing.
¡ Step 4: Hardware executes instructions and moves data to get results.
¡ Step 5: Computation is completed and result Y is returned to the application.

CPU: Optimize Latency of a Small Number of Complex Threads
Five-Stage Instruction Pipeline

¡ Perfect Pipeline
¡ One instruction completes per cycle after filling 
the pipeline.
¡ No bubbles and maximum throughput.
¡ For N instructions and M stages:
¡ Total Cycles = M + N – 1
¡ Average throughput
= N / (M + N - 1) instructions per cycle
¡ Instruction throughput per second                    
Frequency * N / (M + N - 1)
CPU: Optimize Latency of a Small Number of Complex Threads
Five-Stage Instruction Pipeline

¡ Any condition that causes the pipeline to 
stall is called a hazard.
¡
Result: Much bubbles and degraded efficiency
¡ Various types of hazards
¡
Data Hazard: Stall due to dependencies of some 
data
¡
Read-after-write (RAW)
¡
Write-after-write (WAW)
¡
Write-after-read (WAR)
¡
Control Hazard: Stall due to branch and 
synchronization
¡
Structural hazard: Stall due to contention on 
hardware such as memory channel, cache slot, 
queue, etc.

Optimization #5: Speculative Execution
¡ Prediction for next instructions
¡
Issue risky instructions on the chance of considerable benefits.
¡ Benefit
¡
Quick completion --- low latency
¡
Keep deep pipeline busy --- high throughput
¡ Cost
¡
Wrong-path work wastes energy and cycles.
¡
Recovery penalty grows with pipeline depth and speculation window.

Speculative Execution: Branch Prediction
¡ Naïve speculative execution: Static Prediction
¡
The compiler resolves user’s codes and find the 
branches that would not be taken.
¡
Remove corresponding instructions to avoid 
control hazards.
¡ Dynamic Branch Prediction
¡
Learn branch behavior autonomously, no 
compiler analysis or profiling
¡
Adapt to changing branch behavior
Example: Why branch is predictable

CPU: Optimize Latency of a Small Number of Complex Threads
Optimization #6: OoO Superscalar with Hyper-Threading
¡ Problem: Even OoO superscalar cores have idle slot issues.
¡ Reasons: 
¡
Cache miss, branch misprediction, dependency chain……
¡ Hyper-threading introduces simultaneous multithreading (SMT)
¡
Multiple hardware threads share one physical core.
¡
Each logical thread has its own architectural state.
¡
Execution units, caches, queues, and predictors are shared.
¡ The closest architecture to modern CPUs.

From CPU to GPU: Parallelism for Huge Computing Power!
¡ CPU’s Goal: Be general to complex tasks.
¡
Hazards are easy to occur, forcing CPU microarchitecture to implement much optimizations.
¡
"Control logic" such as branches and dependencies in complex tasks incur many synchronization among 
cores.
¡
Result: Scale to hundreds of heavy cores.
¡ GPU’s Goal: Be specific to tasks that are easy to parallel.
¡
Control logic is less, data parallelism is easy.
¡
Example: vector processing.
¡
Result: Scale to 1,000s to 10,000s of light cores.
¡
10x to 100x of computing power than CPU!
Difference of Scaling Cores: Control vs. Compute

GPU: Optimize Throughput of a Large Number of Simple Threads
¡
Hundreds of Streaming Multiprocessors
(SM)s
¡
Each SM consists of:
¡
Processing units, e.g., INT32, FP32, FP64, etc.
¡

¡

Warp Scheduler
¡
When deploy multiple threads, GPU packages a 
branch of threads into a warp.
¡
The scheduler decides which warp would run at one 
time slot, and these threads shard a register file.
¡
When one warp waits, schedule another ready warp.
¡
High-speed shared memory for intra-SM data 
exchange.
¡
Tensor core: accelerator for matrix operations.

CPU Multicore Programming: pThread
¡ Break down a complex task into multiple lightweight sub-tasks.
¡
One process contains multiple threads. 
¡
Threads share the same virtual address space, global variables and heap objects are shared.
¡
Synchronization is the programmer’s responsibility. 
Thread Parallelism with Shared Memory Programming Model

CPU Multicore Programming: pThread
¡
Example
¡ sum += local_sum;
¡ For each thread
¡ Load sum
¡ Add local_sum
¡ Store sum
¡
If two threads execute concurrently
¡ both may read the old value; 
¡ both compute new values; 
¡ one write overwrites the other. 
¡ Race Conditions: multiple threads access a 
shared resource and final result depends on 
timing. 
¡ A critical section is code that must be 
executed by only one thread at a time.
Race Condition and Critical Section

CPU Multicore Programming: pThread
¡ Mutex pattern:
Mutex: Protect Shared State
pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
sum += local_sum;
pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);
¡ The Mutex provides:
¡ Serialized access to critical section 
¡ Race avoidance for protected 
shared state 
¡ Cost: Lock contention
Only one thread holds the mutex; others wait and the protected region is serialized

CPU Multicore Programming: pThread
¡ Barrier: All threads wait until everyone 
reaches the same point.
¡
Use cases: phase-based algorithms, 
debugging, iterative solvers, etc.

Performance Models
¡ Upper Bound: Hardware Throughput
¡
Real Performance: Limited by Load Imbalance, Pipeline Efficiency, and Memory Access
¡ Speedup of a parallel program
¡
P = The number of cores
¡
T(1) = Serial running time
¡
T(P) = Parallel running time
¡
Speedup = T(1) / T(P)
¡ Efficiency = Speedup / P
Performance Is Not Peak FLOPs
¡ Speedup and efficiency usually vary with problem 
size and the number of involved cores

Performance Models
¡ When problem size is fixed, even a small serial fraction caps total speedup
Amdahl's Law: The Serial Fraction Wins
S(p) = 1 / ((1 - f) + f / p)
f: parallelizable fraction
1 - f: serial fraction
p: number of processors / threads
NUMERICAL INTUITION
f = 0.90
max speedup -> 10x
f = 0.99
max speedup -> 100x
